How to Reward Vulnerability Wins
Vulnerability has its own intrinsic rewards over time. In the
meantime, you can make their efforts obvious to others, offer
encouragement, and show appreciation for small and large
strides along the way. So, while you are maturing your
vulnerability practice and waiting for the intrinsic rewards to
kick in, take time to recognize individual and team efforts to let
their guard down.
Recognize Vulnerability Wins:
• “Wins” are currency: Did an individual or the whole team
known for working solo ask for help? Did it have a
positive impact on a challenging deliverable? Invite the
team to share their success story at the next all team
meeting. Try Workshop #3 to prepare for the all hands.
• Create a Vulnerability Memory Board: In the early days,
teams may not recognize the progress they are making.
Or they may show vulnerable moments and then
regress to presenting their old cold-hearted steely
armours. Create a Vulnerability Memory Board to
remind the teams of their progress. For a maturing team
who has done Vulnerability Circles (Worksheet V1) at
the beginning of their practice, hold another one and ask
them how it feels different than that first time.
• Worksheet V1 Gone Sticky: Use the Vulnerability Circle
Worksheet V1 and the “Feeling Stuck” scenario below
to practice asking for help sooner rather than later when
we are “stuck”.

share your own challenge and ask for specific help -
without calling yourself a dummy. Ask if anyone else on
the team is feeling stuck and give them space to
practice asking for help while making it specific - and
without self-deprecation.
Appreciation is a great reward!! Thank the helpers, the
askers, and the team for unblocking important work.
"Feeling Stuck" Scenario:
• Vulnerability WIN: "I'm hitting a wall on this
[specific task]. Has anyone tackled something

perspective? Or maybe there's a resource I'm

• Vulnerability FAIL: "I'm so dumb, I can't figure this
out, and I'm going to get fired.”
Why it’s important: Asking for help is powerful especially
when it is specific. Self-deprecation shuts down
support. Focusing on the actual problem lets someone
offer the needed assistance. Don’t forget to thank your
helper!
Take time to reward teams and individuals who changed
their outlooks from maintaining a tough exterior to inviting
collaboration, laughing at their own mistakes, and taking
risks.

How to Celebrate Vulnerability
There are always moments in a new practice when we revert to
the old ways of working. Celebrating our awareness of our
backslides removes blame and encourages learning. This extra
step can harden the connection between vulnerability and
engagement.
• Celebrate the Backslides: If we can name a backslide,
we can learn from it. And we can learn from each other’s
backslides. Try Worksheet V2 and rename it Backslide
Stories.
• Add Backslide Moments to the Vulnerability Memory
Board created in the last section.
• Celebrate the Trendline: What are some ways you can
quantify how vulnerability is making a positive
difference? Have we reduced the time we stew over a
challenge by asking for help? Have we reduced rework
by stepping out of our siloes and collaborating with
another team? When we sent a team member home
who is tending to a sick loved one, did we feel energized
and happy about adding their work to the team’s
workload? These are proper milestones in our
vulnerability maturity. Celebrate them visibly on the
Vulnerability Memory Board.

Vulnerability

How to Sustain Vulnerability
Turns out, the best teams fight constructively. Research by
Jennifer Mueller of the University of San Diego shows that a
little respectful conflict fuels creative solutions precisely
because everyone's not afraid to butt heads in service of a
better outcome. When you're not wasting energy hiding
mistakes, those disagreements become catalysts for success,
not nails in the coffin of team morale. Let’s try some
constructive conflict scenarios here:
The Constructive Clash Scenario
• Vulnerability WIN: "I respect your approach, but
here's why I think [alternative] might be a stronger
play, based on [data or past experience].
• Vulnerability FAIL: "This whole idea is terrible, you
always do it this way and it always fails, what's wrong
with you?"
Why it Matters: Respectful disagreement fuels growth, but
there's a difference between challenging ideas and
attacking the person behind them.
Have the constructive clash in private. Then role play the
clash together using Worksheet V3 to celebrate
constructive feedback. Encourage team members to
practice what they saw.
Don’t underestimate the ripple effect of sustained vulnerability!
Studies prove that customers can sense the difference
between a team operating from fear and one energized by that
sense of safety and shared purpose.

Vulnerability

How to Rescue Failing Vulnerability
Practices
Vulnerability + Professionalism Gotta Coexist: Fostering
vulnerability doesn't mean turning the workplace into a non-
stop group therapy session. Here's how to strike that balance:
• Boundaries Matter, Even When You're Real:
Vulnerability in the service of the team isn't an excuse
for oversharing. Guidelines are king! Think specific
work-related challenges ("This new process is driving
me nuts"), admitting knowledge gaps ("I need help on
this..."), or owning up to missteps that impacted others.
Keep personal life drama, venting about annoying
coworkers, or armchair psychologist moments for
outside work hours.
• Sharing with Purpose, Not Just to Complain:
Vulnerability is a tool, not a whine-fest. Focus on
solutions or what you're LEARNING from a tough
experience. "This project's a mess, and here's where I
think I messed up" opens a productive door. "This project
sucks" slams it shut.
• Respect is the Bedrock:
Empathy doesn't mean tolerating unprofessional
behavior. It's okay to have hard conversations even
amidst a culture of honesty. Leaders, especially, need to
model this – they still hold people accountable. The

Vulnerability

difference? It's not humiliating; it's clear, specific, and
focused on finding a better way forward together.
• HR managers, Step Up Your Game: Lip service to
vulnerability doesn’t hack it. Your HR team needs to be
trained to support employees choosing vulnerability.
They should be champions of fairness, not enforcers of
rigid rules.

The "What's My Job Now?" Moment Scenario
• Vulnerability WIN: [Addressing their team] "Alright folks,
this shift to [new process] is a big change. I'm still

what I'm thinking so far, but open to your input on what
would be most helpful."
• Vulnerability FAIL: "I have no idea how I'm useful
anymore. This new system sucks, and I'm lost. Anyone
else feel the same?"
Why it Matters: Admitting uncertainty humanizes you. Following
immediately with proactive steps to find your place in the new

system sets an important example. It invites collaboration
instead of inviting everyone to a pity party.
When you model how to respond to big changes to your role,
you may be giving them one of the best lessons in their
professional careers. When you share your thoughts and ask
for their input, you are building trust that you have a plan on
how to bounce back and want to help them be resilient to the
change as well. Your vulnerability will definitely impact their own
response to the current change and can teach them how to
respond to changes in the future.
The Overburdened Buffer Scenario
• Vulnerability WIN: [To their superior] "I'm getting pulled
in many directions with these changes. I need help
prioritizing which requests from my team are essential

bottleneck, not the facilitator."
• Vulnerability FAIL: [Exhausted & exasperated] "I'm just
the messenger getting yelled at from both sides! No one
gets how hard this is. Should I just give everyone your
direct contact so you can all fight it out?"
Why it Matters: Asking for strategic support is vulnerable and
is highly effective when you frame it as essential support
needed to help your teams be successful. Venting may be
tempting, but ultimately makes managers look ineffective.

Forging Trust in the Vault
How Titan National Bank Built a Culture Where Vulnerability
Wasn't a Liability.
The Challenge: Titan National Bank was steady as an old safe
– and just as change-resistant. Processes were rigid, hierarchy
ruled, and while employees rarely screwed up publicly, neither
did they take the calculated risks that could lead to truly
innovative services. Then, those pesky fintech upstarts started
chipping away at their market share. Titan's leadership realized
that a bunker mentality wouldn't cut it anymore – they needed
a team that felt secure enough to suggest crazy ideas, own up
to mistakes quickly, and navigate inevitable client frustrations
with empathy instead of defensiveness.
The Vulnerability Offensive:
• Leader's Under the Microscope: No more pretending
the CEO had all the answers. She began company-wide
meetings by admitting a recent strategic fumble,
followed by what she was doing differently because of it.
This set off a chain reaction, with managers hesitantly
(then boldly) following suit.

Vulnerability

• The Fail Fest: Not a pity party! These were short,
snappy, even humorous team spotlights on how a
misstep led to unexpected improvement. It began with
showcasing "safe" process tweaks, but quickly
escalated to admitting client relationship blunders,
showing that honesty was rewarded, not career-ending.
• "Help Wanted" Brainstorm Boards: Instead of agonizing
in silos, teams posted challenges on a dedicated space
(physical and digital). Asking for help became
normalized, and those who offered a fresh perspective
were publicly praised – even when their solution wasn't
the final winner.
• The "Feelings...with Follow-Through" Approach: Leaders
focused on reframing empathy. It wasn't about coddling
upset clients, but channeling their frustration into
actionable changes. Employees were taught to say, "I
understand that's incredibly frustrating. Here's what I
CAN do, and what I'll take to my team to find a better
way..."
The Impact:
• Ideas That Seemed Nuts, but Worked: A bored teller
turned social media whiz revamped their online
presence with sassy, informative posts, attracting a
younger clientele. A branch manager's "wild idea" for a
community outreach program built stronger local
business partnerships than expensive conventional
advertising.

Vulnerability

• Screw-Ups Didn't Derail: A botched regulatory reporting
error was caught early because the team member
responsible fessed up, allowing for immediate
correction. This led to revamping overly complex
procedures that were setting everyone up for potential
failure.
• Client Loyalty Got Stickier: Turns out, when customers
felt truly heard – even when the answer was "no" – the
relationship remained strong. Complaints on review
sites decreased, and referrals from existing clients
increased due to proactive problem-solving and honest
communication, even in tough situations.
Key Takeaway:
Building vulnerability-as-strength into a conservative industry
like banking isn't easy. Titan Bank learned that it's not about
"sharing feelings" but tangible actions that prove they trust their
people to handle the tough stuff. Respect is paramount, and
that meant clear guidelines, support systems, and follow-
through on those moments of vulnerability to show that taking
those risks is how everyone wins.
Additional Thoughts:
Vulnerability in Action for the Banking Sector
• Cybersecurity Breaches: The instinct is to hide
mistakes, fearing reputational damage. But, a culture of
quickly admitting issues leads to faster containment and
mitigation. Train employees to immediately escalate

anomalies, however minor, with the promise of focusing

• Client Data Concerns: Instead of defensive legalese

Enablement

ENABLEMENT
Why is Enablement Critical to
Employee Engagement?
Empowering employees to make decisions and enabling them
to do their work with the latest tools and technologies boosts
engagement. It gives them a sense of ownership in their
organizations’ solutions and the sense their work is connected
to the greater “Why”. It is about clearing the path so your people
can charge forward, unblocked by bureaucracy, legacy
technologies, and outdated policies. It allows them to optimize
workflows for delivery to customers and ensures all employees
feel their voice MATTERS in this process.
A study by Kotter International found a 682% average increase
in revenue growth for 12 organizations with performance-
enhancing cultures.

Enablement

KEY OUTCOME
People don't just feel heard, they feel UNSTOPPABLE. They
know leadership no longer tolerates roadblocks and is actively
clearing the way for their efforts to truly shine. They feel their
organization is delegating effectively and setting their
employees up for success.

Enablement

How to Model Enablement
Employees look to their managers to empower them with the
tools, technology, information and training they need to do their
jobs. They also need the authority to make the decisions that
require their specific knowledge to make the right decision for
the desired outcome. Managers can optimize engagement
using important enablement moves:
• Connect the work to the “Why”
• Remove barriers
• Optimize ways of working for efficient performance
• Use knowledge where the work happens to make
decisions about that work
• Identify Legacy Practices that block work
• Remove legacy practices that hinder progress
• Prioritize high impact projects

Connect the Work to the “Why”:
Managers, you are your employee’s connection to the higher
purpose of their organizations.

and keep morale from nosediving when setbacks

Unleashing Potential at Frontline Retail – How One Company

The Challenge: Horizon Sales was a mid-sized retailer of
sporting goods with a classic problem: they knew their frontline
employees were the key to exceptional customer experiences,
yet those employees felt undervalued, micromanaged, and
burnt out. Turnover was high, especially among their most
enthusiastic new hires, and morale was dismal despite
attempts at generic "Employee Appreciation" events. This
wasn't just impacting their bottom line but also their ability to
adapt as e-commerce began stealing market share. Horizon's
leadership realized a shift was urgently needed; they couldn't
just offer better prices; they needed a stellar in-store
experience to remain competitive.
The "Enablement" Revolution
Instead of the usual jargon-filled pronouncements about a new
focus on "empowerment," Horizon made it clear this was going
to be about action, not posters. Here's how they tackled those

core obstacles that get in the way of teams truly owning their
work:
Busting Bureaucratic Bottlenecks
o Death to the Dress Code: Their outdated uniform policy
was more suited for 1950s office drones than a team
selling activewear. They replaced it with broad
guidelines (brand colors, safety-focused), and let
individuals express themselves within those. The impact
was immediate – employees felt more comfortable,
which translated to confidence when interacting with
customers.
o "Power to the Pricing Guns": Employees were given the
authority to offer small discounts on the spot to close a
sale, resolve minor customer complaints, or price match
within set parameters. This eliminated the need to
escalate every little thing to a manager, speeding up
transactions and making employees feel trusted.
Growth Beyond Job Titles
o Mastering Their Domain: Horizon invested in product-
specific training, turning staff into mini-experts. A runner
wasn't just stocking shoes but could advise on the best
fit for terrain and customer goals. This fueled
enthusiasm, and those product deep-dives frequently
led to increased upsells.
o Sharing the Knowledge: Instead of relying solely on
outside trainers, they implemented a mentorship

o Scheduling Sanity: Instead of auto-generated shifts,
managers were required to have 1:1 conversations
about schedule preferences. Balancing part-timer
availability with peak hours remained a challenge, but
incorporating input boosted morale and decreased "no
call, no show" absences.
o Time Theft...From Themselves: Mandatory unpaid

delivered in short huddles at shift changeover,
minimizing the feeling that their personal time wasn't
valued.
Making the Work...Work BETTER
o "Suggestion Box" Revamp: The dusty box was replaced

o Tech Tools that Don't Suck: They finally admitted their

sales and employee frustration. Investing in a

streamlined UI with dedicated training time had a

While writing this book, we often got stuck on how best to share
a particular practice with you. Often one of us woke up with a

is often the pause that boosts creativity. It surprises us with new
connections that were not obvious to us while we were awake.
Edison had a favorite chair for what we like to call his
innovation naps. He carefully staged his naps to capture
new ideas. Before his nap, Edison placed a metal bowl

beside his favorite chair so that his hand holding a metal
ball hung directly over it. When he entered REM sleep,
his muscles relaxed, and his hand released the metal
ball - which hit the metal pan with a loud clang! He
promptly woke up to write down the new solutions he
had discovered during his sleep – yes, he kept writing
supplies handy for this purpose. In REM sleep, Edison’s
brain connected the new information he was exploring
before his nap to already existing information stored in
his brain. Your brain does this too!

#1 Pitfall: ONE SIZE FITS ALL

Let's be honest – there's no magic formula to make change
easy. But here are some strategies to combat those classic
obstacles and increase your odds of those bright ideas actually
seeing the light of day instead of fizzling out:
• "We Don't Have Time" Syndrome: Change needs
dedicated time and resources. If it's always an
afterthought tacked onto everyone's overflowing plate,
progress crawls, or worse, never even begins. Try
Worksheet R1.
• Call in the Demo Crew: Don't just talk about potential
solutions, prototype them! Try a rough mock-up of a new
workflow or a role-playing session to test-drive a new
client interaction.

Reflection

Stuck in Perfection Paralysis: Waiting for the flawless,
everyone-agrees masterplan turns into a convenient
excuse for inaction. Sometimes, a messy start is better
than no start at all. Try Worksheet R2.
• The Accountability Void: Everyone nods enthusiastically
when a new process is proposed, but who's actually
responsible for making it happen? When ownership is
vague, so is follow-through.
Name Names: Who is the "champion" of this initiative?
They don't need to do all the work, but they own making
sure progress happens.
Public accountability is surprisingly powerful! Resource
Reallocation: Need to free up someone's time to focus
on the change? Be clear about what gets deprioritized
to make that happen. Good intentions don't pay the bills;
strategic choices do.
Small Wins = Big Motivation: Break down that ambitious
goal into bite-sized milestones. Celebrate each one
visibly! This keeps spirits up when the end goal still feels
a million miles away. Try Worksheet R3.
• The "Pre-Mortem" Experiment: Force teams to be
brutally honest about why this initiative might fail.
Addressing those potential pitfalls early on can make the
execution far smoother. Fear of the Unknown: Even a
much-needed change can be scary. Fear disguised as
skepticism kills momentum. ("That'll never work
because..."). Try Worksheet R4.
• Embrace Imperfect Pilots: Launch a "test and tweak"
version of that new process. Gather real-world data

Reflection

quickly to prove what works and what needs fixing,
without overplanning it. Try Worksheet R5.
• Track the Transformation: Have a visual reminder of the
progress (even with setbacks!). A simple timeline with
milestones reinforces the sense that this change isn't
just talk, it's happening. Try Worksheet R3 or R4.
Dealing with the Change Deniers
Even with the best planning, there will be those who cling to the
old ways, convinced any change is doomed. Address their
resistance with powerful questions without getting dragged into
negativity:
• The "Why Does It Matter Chatter”: Instead of defending
your brilliant plan, ask them; "If this problem remains
unsolved, what's the consequence for you/your
team/our clients?" Focus on the pain point they DO care
about.
• Harness Their Pessimism: They're great at spotting
potential failures! Channel that negative energy by
asking; "How can we mitigate this risk?" Often, they have
valuable insights, even if their delivery is less than
inspiring.
• Invite, Don't Impose: Critiquing from afar is easy. Turn
the distracting background noise into a bit of ownership
by asking: “Can you be a part of the pilot project?” Often
they are remaining on the fringe and don’t know how to
shift their perspective. Try Worksheet R3.

Reflection

Remember, Sometimes Slow is Strategic:
Time is on your side! Not everyone needs to be an early adopter
for change to be successful. Focus on getting those with
influence onboard, and let the results eventually sway the
stubborn holdouts.
• The Power of Progress Reports (That Aren't Boring)
Chuck the Corporate-Speak: No one reads those 20-
page updates full of jargon. Infographics, quick video
snippets, even a "highlight reel" of small wins are far
more impactful, especially for busy higher-ups. Use your
Knowledge Hub for this!
• Own the Setbacks: Got off track? Don't sugarcoat it.
Briefly state the problem, the course correction, and
why you're confident it won't derail the whole project.
Transparency builds trust. (Worksheet #4)
• Celebrate the "Unsung Heroes": Who went above and
beyond to solve that unexpected glitch? Public
recognition not only rewards those change-makers, it
inspires others. Use your Knowledge Hub to capture
recognition after acknowledging contributions in a
public forum with the teams.
The Bottom Line: From “Aha!” to Outcomes
Turn those "Aha!" moments from workshops and reflection
sessions into tangible outcomes that make everyone's work
lives better – THAT'S the true test of whether transformation
efforts are worth it. Stop chasing some abstract ideal of change

Reflection

and prove, one step at a time, that struggles lead to payoffs
worth fighting for.

Reflection

Objective
Designate a time for employees to reflect on their week's work, both
the highs and the lows.
Materials Needed
Quiet space
Notebooks or digital note-taking tools
Steps
1. Schedule a specific hour each week for reflection.
2. Prepare optional questions to guide the reflection:
• What was the highlight of your week?
• What might you have done differently?
3. Model it to Coach it! Tell your own reflection story.
1. How a reflection this week impacted/helped you
4. Ask team members to jot down their reflections
Reflection
o Recall how your reflection affected your engagement with
your work and your colleagues (Step 3).
o Ask the team, “How did pausing to reflect affect your
mindset, approach to work, and engagement levels?”
Worksheet R1: The Reflection Hour

Reflection

Objective
Surface potential problems early and brainstorm creative fixes.
Steps
1. Keep it low-tech! This is NOT about polished presentations.
Use whiteboard sketches, hand-drawn flowcharts, sticky
notes... whatever gets the rough idea across quickly.
2. Choose a discussed new process, communication channel,
or client-facing initiative that hasn't gained traction.
3. Brainstorm the User Experience Task everyone to think
through the change from the perspective of those who'd be
most impacted (employees, customers, etc.). Walk through
each step as if YOU were the one using the new system.
4. Embrace Constructive Chaos: Get those creative juices
flowing! Applaud poking holes, laughing at flawed elements,
and brainstorming workarounds on the fly.
Reflection
o Did the act of prototyping reveal obstacles unseen in
theoretical discussions?
o Which parts of the change seem surprisingly easy to implement
after this visualization?
o Key Takeaway: Done is better than perfect, and a tangible start,
even a messy one, often fuels better ideas than another round
of planning.
Worksheet R2: The "Make It Real" Mock-Up

Reflection

Objective:
Clearly name owners and support roles to free a change initiative
from the "everyone's responsible, so no one is" trap.
Steps:
1. Select a change initiative with potential solutions but no actions.
2. Name That Champion: Name a single person who is ultimately
responsible for driving the change forward. The owner is the
point person for progress: they do not do all the work.
3. The Support Squad: Name specific roles who can provide
expertise, resources, or approval to make the change happen.
4. Timeline: Break the initiative into milestones with deadlines, even
if tentative.
Reflection
o Was it harder than expected to agree on that "champion"? This
exposes hidden hesitation about the idea itself.
o Are there resource gaps?
o Is the team promising support that they can realistically deliver
without a shift in priorities?
o Is the timeline realistic?
o Key Takeaway: Accountability isn't about assigning blame, but
about giving a good idea the structure it needs to succeed.
Worksheet R3: The Accountability Assignment

Reflection

Objective:
Proactively brainstorm solutions to potential pitfalls that could derail
a proposed change.
Steps:
1. Select a proposed change with buy-in and lurking fears about
ways it could go sideways.
2. Assume Disaster: The project has crashed and burned. Task
everyone to list ALL the reasons why, from the plausible to the
outlandish.
3. Reverse Engineer the Rescue: For each item on the "failure list",
brainstorm ways to prevent or minimize the damage.
4. The Reality Check:
o Are some of those risks so great that the whole idea needs
rethinking?
Is it better to face this now, rather than after time and
resources have been wasted?
Reflection:
o Gut Check: Was the group overly optimistic initially?
o Did we find some change champions who are secretly terrified
and need additional support to feel confident moving forward?
o Key Takeaway: Smart pessimism is an act of self-preservation
Worksheet R4: The Pre-Mortem Panic Session

Reflection

Objective:
Embrace the mindset that adjusting the initial plan doesn't equal
failure. In fact, it can assure success! Agility is key!
Steps:
1. Choose a project that needs to deviate from the original plan.
2. Analyze the Roadblock: Clearly define what's NOT working,
avoiding blame and focusing on systems/processes.
3. The "What If" Brainstorm: Throw out wild alternative solutions.
The focus is on quantity, not quality, at this stage.
4. Vetting the Madness: Now, pick the TOP 3 most promising
alternatives and briefly look at the pros, cons, and what would
be needed to implement each.
Reflection:
o Did anyone resist course correction initially? Why?
o Did the brainstorm uncover an unexpectedly simple tweak
that could be a game-changer?
o Key Takeaway: Success isn't about rigidly sticking to the plan;
it's about reaching the destination, even if you take a few
scenic detours.

Being aware of change fatigue is an important part of understanding

Reflection

How a Government IT Helpdesk Used
Reflection to Stop Drowning in Tickets
Picture this: a government agency's IT department is
perpetually caught in a tsunami of helpdesk tickets. Password
resets, malfunctioning printers from the Clinton era, glitchy
software updates forced upon them without warning... the
classics. Urgent infrastructure modernization projects keep
getting pushed back while they play whack-a-mole with a
thousand minor annoyances. Morale is in the basement,
burnout is rampant, and even the most dedicated techs are
starting to feel like glorified reboot monkeys. That was the grim
reality facing the IT team at a large state-level agency…until
they started reflecting in a way that led to change.
Step 1: Beyond the Helpdesk Ticket Abyss
The usual "employee satisfaction surveys" were useless here.
Sure, everyone was miserable, but those surveys didn't provide
the granular data needed to pinpoint why. Here's how they got
specific:
• Ticket Time-Sponge Audit: For one brutal week, every
tech meticulously tracked where their time truly went –
not just vague categories, but down to "15 minutes

Reflection

helping Sandra in accounting figure out why the 'any
key’ won't print."
• Problem Patterns: They took it beyond individuals to the
systems they used. Were 60% of tickets due to a buggy
new system? Was there a spike after specific software
patches? Suddenly root causes started to emerge.
• The "Frustration Scale": Alongside each ticket, techs
rated their frustration level, and why. Was it a simple fix
but made infuriating by outdated documentation? This
added a less quantifiable, but equally important, layer of
insight.
Step 2: From Data Dump to Actionable Insights
Leadership's initial reaction was panic – the raw data was a
horror show. But instead of finger-pointing, they focused on
themes:
• The "Death by a Thousand Papercuts" Problem: Many
infuriating tickets were minor, but collectively consumed
vast amounts of time. Could they automate password
resets, or create a user-friendly troubleshooting portal
with those super basic fixes?
• Silo Suffering: Turns out, the recent software "upgrade"
hadn't included essential training for IT, let alone end-
users. How can the IT Helpdesk team and end users be
included in the roll-out process to avoid messy clean-
ups afterward.
• Hero Culture Backfires: A few superstar techs were
single-handedly keeping the system afloat, while

Reflection

harboring massive resentment. Many were on the verge
of quitting. Can we standardize knowledge sharing and
improve documentation? What will happen if our heroes
take their brilliance elsewhere?
Step 3: Reflection + Real Authority = Progress
The IT team's insights and proposed solutions only mattered
because leadership was receptive. The sheer severity of the
crisis forced soul searching at the top. Here's what changed:
• IT Gets a Seat at the Table: They were included in high-
level planning meetings, not as afterthought, but to
prevent those roll-outs that spawned a thousand
helpdesk nightmares.
• Budget Battles: IT got a bit more muscle to push for
necessary upgrades instead of being stuck in an
endless patch-and-pray cycle. Were they suddenly flush
with cash? Nope, but some strategic wins proved their
point.
• Kill the Zombie Projects: A hard look at the backlog
revealed projects that could be mercifully axed, or at
least de-prioritized. This freed up brainpower for those
truly impactful improvements.
The Impact (It Wasn't Overnight Magic)
• Ticket volume decreased. Not because citizens
magically became tech-savvy, but due to targeted self-
help tools and behind-the-scenes fixes that prevented
common errors.

Reflection

• Morale improved... cautiously. Suddenly, techs were
fixing root causes, not just putting Band-Aids on a
perpetually crashing system. This built a sense of
agency lacking before.
• Proactive, Not Just Reactive: Could they anticipate the
next roll-out disaster? Sometimes. This is where the
strengthened relationship with other departments due to
the improved communication became key for the IT
team
Key Takeaway: In a government setting, especially IT, change
is often agonizingly slow. But, by structuring reflection around
actionable data points, and engaging a leadership team that is
truly shocked by what was found, this department stopped
drowning and maybe, just maybe, began to lay the groundwork
for a 21st century IT operation.

Appendix

Making the Case for a Culture Shift
In today's fast-paced business environment, many
organizations prioritize financial metrics, technological
upgrades, or cost reductions. While undeniably important,
these elements often overshadow the most critical competitive
strategy: organizational culture.
Why Your Organization’s Culture Matters
When culture thrives, employees are more engaged, teams are
more cohesive, customers are more loyal, and businesses are
more resilient. When culture thrives, organizations thrive!
Ignoring culture, on the other hand, can result in a disengaged
workforce, low morale, and eventually, financial downturns.
Your Call-to-Action: Make the Case for a Culture Shift
To enact meaningful change, you'll first need to make a
compelling case for a culture-centric approach within your
organization.
Leadership across the organization needs to:
1. Evaluate Current Culture: Utilize employee surveys and
interviews to assess the state of your current culture.
2. Identify Pain Points: Use the collected data to pinpoint areas
that require immediate attention.

3. Compile Benefits: Research and compile the benefits of a
strong organizational culture.
4. Present to Leadership: Create a compelling presentation to
showcase your findings and recommendations to the
organization's leadership.

How to Read This Book
This book is short on purpose.
No frameworks. No worksheets. Just observations.
Patterns that show up in company after company.
Conversations that happened too late. Signals that were
there but went unnoticed.
This book is for anyone who's ever been surprised by a
resignation. For the executive who thought retention was
fine until three senior people quit in the same quarter.
For the manager who's trying to keep a team together
without the tools or visibility to see what's actually
happening.
Each entry stands alone. Read them in order or skip to
whatever title pulls you in. Some will land immediately.
Others won't matter until someone on your team resigns
and you remember something you read here.

How to read this book

The goal isn't to give you a system. It's to change what you
see.
Most books about retention tell you what to do. This one
shows you what you're not seeing.
The title is the thesis: by the time you know someone's
leaving, they're already gone. The decision was made. You
just weren't in the room.
You'll recognize some of these stories. You might have lived
them. You might be living one right now without knowing it.
If you finish this book and start paying attention to the quiet
person in your next meeting, it worked.

Four Months Before
A senior engineer never told his manager he was thinking
about leaving.
Except he did. Four months before he resigned.
His manager didn't hear it that way. He heard a question
about promotion paths. Replied with "we'll figure it out."
The engineer heard something different. He heard: you're
not a priority.
He stopped pushing. Started taking recruiter calls instead.
His manager found out the day he resigned. Asked if there
was anything that could change his mind.
There wasn't. That conversation happened four months
too late.
Why didn't he push harder? Make it clearer he was
serious?

The 4X Rule
Here's a simple way to estimate what turnover is actually
costing you: take whatever number you're using now and
multiply it by four.
If your finance team says turnover cost $500K last year,
the real number is closer to $2M.
This isn't a guess. It's what shows up consistently when
companies actually measure the full cost: recruiting,
onboarding, ramp time, lost productivity, knowledge loss,
management overhead, project delays, client disruption.
Most companies only measure the first two. The other six
are invisible in their systems.
The 4X rule isn't precise. Some roles cost more. Senior
technical hires can run 300-400% of salary. Sales roles
with established client relationships can be even higher.
Entry-level positions might be closer to 100%.
But as a baseline, 4X gets you in the right neighborhood.
Close enough to change how you think about the problem.
If you've been treating turnover as a $500K issue, you've
been underinvesting in prevention by about $1.5M.

Then the new person arrives, and the clock doesn't stop.

One person leaves. Then another.
By the time you notice the pattern, you're not dealing with
turnover anymore. You're dealing with a cascade.

member leaves, the people who remain start asking
questions. Why did she leave? What does she know that I
don't? Is something happening here that I should be
worried about?
Even if the answers are innocent, the questions are
corrosive. They plant seeds of doubt that grow into job
searches.
The math compounds quickly. If one departure has a 15%
chance of triggering another, and that departure has the

same odds, a single resignation can set off a chain reaction

When you calculate turnover cost, you're measuring

Ghost Working
Before someone resigns, there's a period where they've
already decided to leave but haven't told anyone yet.
During this time, they're still showing up. Still attending
meetings. Still collecting a paycheck. But they're not fully

isn't.
The period can last weeks or months. For the employee
who spent four months deciding to leave, that's four
months of diminished output. Not zero output. Just less
than what you were paying for.

isn't doing anything wrong, exactly. They're just not doing
their best work. The difference is subtle enough to miss but
expensive enough to matter.
If 10% of your workforce is ghost working at any given

resigned. You're paying for presence, not performance.

The Annual Survey Problem
Once a year, companies send out an engagement survey.
Employees answer questions about how they feel. The
results get compiled into a report. Leadership reviews the
report. Action plans get created.
By the time any of this happens, the data is already stale.
The employee who was frustrated in March filled out the
survey. By June, when the results came back, she'd
already accepted another offer. The survey captured how
she felt four months ago. It didn't capture that she was
leaving.
Annual surveys measure a moment in time. They don't
measure movement. They can tell you that 73% of
employees felt supported last quarter. They can't tell you
that three of your best engineers have interviews
scheduled for next week.
The cadence is wrong. Engagement doesn't change once
a year. It changes constantly. Someone gets passed over
for a promotion and their engagement drops that week.
Someone's manager leaves and their engagement drops
that month. By the time the annual survey catches it, the
damage is done.
Annual surveys aren't useless. They're just too slow to
prevent anything.

Data That Arrives Too Late
The best time to intervene is before someone decides to
leave. The second best time is while they're still deciding.
The worst time is after the decision is made.
Most engagement data arrives at the worst time.
Quarterly surveys tell you how people felt last quarter. Exit
interviews tell you why someone left after they've already
gone. Both are backward-looking. Useful for
understanding patterns over time. Useless for preventing
the resignation that's about to happen.
The manager who could have had a conversation three
weeks ago doesn't have the data. The executive who could
have approved the promotion last month doesn't know it
mattered. Everyone finds out at the same moment: when
the resignation letter arrives.
By then, it's too late. Not too late to learn. Too late to act.
The problem isn't that companies don't collect data. They
collect plenty. The problem is that the data arrives after the
decision has already been made. It's a rearview mirror
when what you need is a windshield.

employees aren't fully honest. Not because they're
dishonest people. Because honesty feels risky
Even when surveys are anonymous, employees don't fully
trust the anonymity. They've heard stories. They know that
a team of four isn't really anonymous. They know that
someone in HR can probably figure out who said what if
they wanted to.
So they hedge. They round up their scores. They say things
are fine when things aren't fine. They save their real
opinions for conversations with friends, with recruiters,
with anyone who can't use the information against them.
The result is data that looks better than reality.
Engagement scores that mask underlying problems. A
false sense of confidence that everything is okay.
The survey says 82% of employees feel valued. Three of
them resign the following month. The survey wasn't wrong,

Section 3

exactly. It just measured what people were willing to say,
not what they actually felt.
The HR Silo
HR knows things. They see the exit interview data and the
turnover patterns. They notice trends across departments
that no individual manager could spot.
But HR doesn't manage anyone's day-to-day work. The
managers do. The managers who don't have access to
most of what HR knows.
This is the silo problem. The people with the data don't
have the relationships. The people with the relationships
don't have the data.
When HR notices that a department has lost four people in
six months, they might flag it in a report. That report might
reach the department head. By then, the fifth person is
already interviewing somewhere else.
The manager on the ground could have intervened earlier.
They know the team. They have the conversations. They
could have noticed the signs and done something about it.
But they didn't have the pattern data. They only saw their
own team, their own interactions, their own slice of the
picture.

Section 3

HR sees the whole picture but can't act on it directly.
Managers can act but can't see the whole picture. The
information exists. It's just in the wrong place at the wrong
time.
Silos don't just slow things down. They make prevention
almost impossible.
Recognition Platforms and 12%
Adoption
The company bought a recognition platform. Employees
can now send each other digital badges. There's a
leaderboard. There are points that can be redeemed for
gift cards.
Three months after launch, adoption is at 12%.
The same people who were already engaged are using it.
The people who weren't engaged before aren't using it
now. The platform didn't change behavior. It just gave the
already-engaged employees a new toy.
This is the recognition platform problem. The tools assume
that recognition isn't happening because it's inconvenient.
Make it easier, and people will do it more.
But convenience wasn't the problem. The problem was
that most managers don't prioritize recognition in the first

Section 3

place. A platform doesn't change that. It just digitizes the
gap.
The 12% who adopted the platform were going to
recognize their people anyway. The 88% who didn't
weren't going to start just because there's an app now.
Six months later, the platform is still live. Almost nobody
uses it. The vendor sends monthly reports showing that
engagement with the platform is declining. The company
quietly stops talking about it.
The problem wasn't the platform. The problem was
thinking that a platform could solve a behavior problem.
The Leadership Offsite That Lasted Two
Weeks
The leadership team went offsite. Two days at a nice hotel.
A facilitator led them through exercises about culture and
engagement.
They came back inspired. There were action items and a
shared document with commitments. Real energy to make
things different.
Two weeks later, everything was back to normal.

Section 3

The action items got deprioritized. The shared document
stopped getting updated. The insights from the offsite
faded as the daily grind took over.
This happens so often it's almost predictable. The offsite
creates a temporary shift in attention. For a few days,
engagement is the priority. Then the quarter closes, or a
client escalates, or a product deadline looms. The urgent
overtakes the important, and the offsite becomes a
memory.
The problem isn't that offsites don't generate good ideas.
They often do. The problem is that nothing sustains the
ideas after the event ends.
Engagement isn't an event. It's a system. You can't fix a
system problem with a two-day workshop. You can only
create the illusion of progress before reverting to the mean.
The offsite felt like action. It wasn't. It was a pause before
returning to the same patterns that created the problem in
the first place.
Training Without Tools
The company invested in manager training. Two days of
workshops on giving feedback and having difficult
conversations.

Section 3

The managers left with new frameworks. New language.
New intentions.
Then they went back to their desks and had the same
number of direct reports, the same number of meetings.
Nothing about their actual capacity had changed.
Training assumes that managers don't do the right things
because they don't know how. Sometimes that's true. More
often, they know what to do. They just don't have the time,
the visibility, or the organizational support to do it.
Teaching a manager how to have a career conversation
doesn't help if they're in meetings eight hours a day.
Showing them how to spot disengagement doesn't help if
they have no visibility into patterns across their team.
Training without tools is like teaching someone to cook
without giving them a kitchen. The knowledge is there. The
capability isn't.
Most manager training fails not because the content is
bad, but because it adds to what managers are supposed
to do without taking anything away. The new skills compete
with everything else on their plate, and everything else
usually wins.

The Engagement Score Nobody Acts
On
The engagement survey came back. The company's score
was 71. That's down two points from last year.
A meeting was scheduled to discuss the results. The
leadership team reviewed the data. They identified three
areas for improvement. They assigned owners to each
area.
Then nothing happened.
Not nothing, exactly. The owners added the items to their
already-full project lists. They had a few conversations.
They drafted some proposals. But the urgent work kept
getting in the way, and the engagement initiatives kept
getting pushed to next month.
By the time the next survey rolled around, the score was
69. Down another two points. The same meeting
happened again. The same areas were identified. The
same owners were assigned.
This is the engagement score trap. The number exists. It
gets reported. It gets discussed. But it rarely drives actual
change.
Part of the problem is that engagement scores don't tell
you what to do. A score of 71 doesn't explain why someone

Section 3

is disengaged or what would make them stay. It's a
symptom, not a diagnosis.
So the score gets noted, the meeting gets held, and the
organization moves on. Until next year, when the score
drops again and everyone wonders why.
Why Your Best Managers Are
Exhausted
Your best managers care. That's what makes them good.
It's also what makes them exhausted.
They're the ones staying late to have the conversation that
might keep someone from leaving. They're the ones
fighting for promotions and raises that the budget doesn't
easily accommodate. They notice when someone seems
off and make time to check in, even when there's no time
to spare.
None of this is in their job description. None of it shows up
in their performance metrics. They do it because they care
about their people, and they know that if they don't do it,
nobody will.
The problem is that caring doesn't scale. A manager can
only have so many difficult conversations in a week. They
can only fight so many battles with leadership. Eventually,
the good ones burn out or give up.

Section 3

When they burn out, they stop doing the invisible work that
kept their team together. When they give up, they become
like every other manager: present but not engaged.
The organization didn't lose a manager. It lost the extra
effort that was holding things together. The effort that was
never measured, never rewarded, and never replaced.
Your best managers are tired because you've made
retention their personal burden instead of an organizational
system.
The Program That Became Paperwork
It started as a good idea. Monthly one-on-ones with a
structured template. Managers would have consistent
conversations with their direct reports. Development
would be tracked. Issues would surface early.
Six months later, the program is paperwork.
Managers fill out the template because they have to. The
conversations follow the form instead of following the
employee. Check the boxes, submit the document, move
on.
The template that was supposed to enable better
conversations has become a substitute for them. The form
gets completed. The actual connection doesn't happen.

Section 3

This is what happens when programs become compliance
exercises. The intention was good. The execution became
bureaucratic. The measure of success shifted from "are
people more engaged" to "did everyone complete the
form."
HR can report that 94% of managers completed their one-
on-ones this quarter. They can't report whether any of
those conversations actually mattered.
The program didn't fail because managers stopped doing
it. It failed because doing it became the goal instead of
what doing it was supposed to achieve.
Paperwork feels like progress. It's easy to track. It's
satisfying to report. But it's not the same as progress. It's
often a substitute for it.
Measuring What's Easy vs. What
Matters
It's easy to measure how many people completed the
training. It's hard to measure whether the training changed
their behavior.
It's easy to measure the engagement survey score. It's
hard to measure whether anyone acted on the results.

Section 3

Companies default to measuring what's easy because
what matters is hard to quantify. So, they build dashboards
full of completion rates and survey scores and turnover
percentages, and they call it visibility.
But these metrics are lagging indicators. They tell you what
already happened. They don't help you change what's
about to happen.
The metrics that would actually matter are harder to
capture. How many people on this team have stopped
asking for growth opportunities? How many have gone
quiet in meetings where they used to speak up?
These patterns exist. They're just not in a dashboard.
They're scattered across hundreds of small moments that
nobody is tracking.
So companies measure what they can and hope it
correlates with what they can't. Sometimes it does. Often
it doesn't. The dashboard looks fine until the day someone
resigns and everyone wonders what they missed.

Section 3

You've tried surveys. You've tried platforms. You've tried
offsites and training and recognition programs.
None of it worked. Not because you didn't care.
Because the solutions weren't designed to solve the
actual problem.
The actual problem isn't that employees are
disengaged. It's that the people closest to them don't
have what they need to do anything about it.
Those people are your managers. They're the ones in
the room when engagement drops. They're the ones
who could intervene if they knew what was happening
and had the support to act.
Instead, they're exhausted and flying blind.
The next section is about them.

The Manager in the Middle

Section 4

Section 4

70% of Engagement, 0% of Tools
Research consistently shows that managers account for
roughly 70% of the variance in employee engagement. The
relationship between an employee and their direct
manager is the single biggest factor in whether they stay
or leave.
Companies know this. They cite the statistic in leadership
meetings. They include it in their manager training decks.
Then they give managers nothing to work with.
No visibility into how their team is actually doing beyond
what people say in one-on-ones. No early warning when

Section 4

someone starts disengaging. No pattern data showing
who's at risk and why. No system for tracking whether the
conversations they're having are making a difference.
Managers get responsibility without capability. They're told
that engagement is their job, and then left to figure it out
with gut instinct and occasional survey scores that arrive
months after the damage is done.
70% of the outcome. 0% of the tools.
When someone leaves, the manager is the one who gets
asked what happened. They're expected to have seen it
coming. They're expected to have done something about
it.
But they were never given what they needed to see it. They
were just given the blame when they didn't.
The Fall Guy
When a key employee resigns, someone has to answer for
it. Usually, that someone is the manager.
Why didn't you see this coming? What could you have done
differently? Did you have regular one-on-ones? Did you
talk about their career path?
The manager sits in the meeting and absorbs the
questions. They don't have good answers because there

Section 4

aren't any. They did have one-on-ones. They did talk about
career paths. None of it was enough, and they don't fully
understand why.
What they can't say is that they raised concerns about this
person's workload three months ago and nothing
changed. They can't say that they've been stretched so
thin managing twelve direct reports that meaningful career
conversations happen once a quarter instead of once a
month.
They can't say any of this because it sounds like excuses.
So they take the blame.
The system failed. The manager becomes the fall guy.
This happens over and over. Good managers absorb
responsibility for outcomes they couldn't control.
Eventually, they stop fighting for things they know won't get
approved. Eventually, some of them leave too.
The fall guy role isn't sustainable. Neither is the system that
creates it.
They Stopped Telling You
There was a time when your team told you things. When
they'd mention frustrations in one-on-ones. When they'd
push back on decisions they disagreed with.

Section 4

Then they stopped.
You might not have noticed when it happened. The silence
arrived gradually. One person stopped raising concerns.
Another stopped asking about promotions.
It felt like progress. Like the team was maturing. Like they'd
finally gotten aligned.
It wasn't progress. They stopped telling you things because
they stopped believing it would help.
Maybe they raised something once and nothing happened.
Maybe they watched a colleague get labeled "difficult" for
pushing back. Maybe they just ran out of energy to fight
battles that never seemed to change anything.
Whatever the reason, the information flow changed. They
still talk to you. They just don't tell you the things that
matter.
The frustrations they used to share with you, they now
share with recruiters. The questions they used to ask you,
they now ask at interviews for other jobs.
You're still having conversations. You're just not in the loop
anymore.

The Request That Died Two Levels Up
The manager knew what the employee needed. A title
change and a salary adjustment. Something concrete that
would address the frustration before it turned into a
resignation.
So they made the request. They wrote the justification.
They sent it up the chain.
Somewhere between their desk and the decision-maker,
the request died. Maybe it got deprioritized. Maybe it got
lost in a queue of other requests. Maybe someone two
levels up decided it wasn't the right time.
The manager never got a clear answer. Just delays. Just
"we'll revisit next quarter." Just silence until they stopped
asking.
The employee never knew any of this happened. They only
knew that they'd asked for something and didn't get it. They
assumed their manager didn't fight for them. Or that the
company didn't value them. Either way, the conclusion was
the same: time to start looking elsewhere.
The manager did everything right. The system failed
anyway.
This is the invisible battle most managers fight. They
advocate for their people and lose. They absorb the loss

Section 4

without being able to explain it. The employee blames them
for an outcome they couldn't control.
Everyone Thinks the System Worked
The employee requested a transfer to a different team. The
manager submitted the paperwork. HR processed the
request. The receiving team said they didn't have
headcount.
Request denied. Everyone followed the process.
Six weeks later, the employee resigned.
From HR's perspective, the system worked. The request
was processed according to policy. From the receiving
team's perspective, they made the right call given their
constraints. From senior leadership's perspective, they
never even knew the request happened.
Nobody did anything wrong. The process was followed.
The outcome was a $200K replacement cost and a
demoralized manager who learned that following the
process doesn't actually help their people.
This is how good systems produce bad outcomes. Every
individual step makes sense in isolation. Every person
involved acted reasonably. The sum of all those reasonable
actions was losing someone who didn't need to be lost.

Section 4

The manager sees the whole picture. They see the
request, the denial, the resignation, the connection
between them. But they can't point to anyone who made a
mistake. The system worked exactly as designed. It just
wasn't designed to prevent turnover.
When everyone thinks the system worked, nobody thinks
they need to fix it.
Reading the Signals Wrong
The employee used to argue in meetings. Now they don't.
The manager notices and feels relieved. Finally, they're
being a team player. Finally, they're not making everything
a debate.
Six weeks later, they resign.
The signal was there. The manager just read it wrong.
This happens constantly. Silence gets interpreted as
agreement. Compliance gets interpreted as buy-in. A drop
in questions gets interpreted as confidence instead of
disengagement.
Managers aren't bad at reading signals because they're
bad managers. They're bad at reading signals because the
signals are ambiguous and they have no baseline for
comparison.

Section 4

When someone goes quiet, it could mean they're focused.
It could mean they're interviewing elsewhere. From the
outside, both look the same.
The only way to know the difference is to have data. To see
patterns over time. To know that this person asked about
their career path four times in Q1 and zero times in Q2.
Managers don't have that data. They have impressions.
They have gut feelings. They have the version of events
that makes the most sense given what they can see.
Usually, the version that makes sense is the optimistic one.
Until it isn't.
"Finally Maturing" vs. Already Gone
The senior engineer used to have opinions about
everything. Technical decisions and process changes.
Always pushing, always advocating for a different
approach.
Then he mellowed out. Started going with the flow.
Stopped being the squeaky wheel.
His manager mentioned it in a leadership meeting. "He's
finally maturing. Less friction, more collaboration."
Two months later, he resigned for a startup that wanted his
opinions.

Section 4

"Finally maturing" is one of the most dangerous phrases in
management. It sounds like growth. It's usually surrender.
The employee didn't mature. They gave up. They stopped
caring enough to fight. They redirected their energy from
trying to change things to planning their exit.
From the outside, maturity and disengagement look
identical. Both involve less conflict. Both involve more
agreement. Both make meetings easier.
The difference is in what's happening underneath. The
mature employee has integrated their concerns and found
peace with the tradeoffs. The disengaged employee has
stopped believing their concerns matter.
Managers can't tell the difference without asking. Without
really asking, in a way that makes honesty safe. Most don't,
because the quiet version is so much easier to manage.
Until it walks out the door.
"Finally Listening" vs. Checked Out
"She's finally listening."
The manager said it with relief. For months, this employee
had been pushing back on the new process. Raising
concerns in every meeting. Questioning decisions that had
already been made.

Section 4

Then she stopped. Started following the process without
complaint. Started nodding in meetings instead of arguing.
The manager thought she'd come around. Thought she'd
finally understood why the changes were necessary.
Thought the resistance phase was over.
It wasn't. The resistance phase had evolved into the
resignation phase.
She hadn't started listening. She'd stopped caring. The
energy she used to spend arguing was now going into job
applications. The concerns she used to raise out loud were
now conversations she had with recruiters.
"Finally listening" and "checked out" produce the same
behavior: compliance. The employee does what's asked
without pushback. Meetings are smoother. Deadlines are
met.
The difference only becomes clear later, when the
resignation arrives and the manager realizes the
compliance wasn't agreement. It was withdrawal.
By then, the listening they thought they'd achieved was
actually silence. The alignment they thought they'd built
was actually distance.

The Confidence Problem
Managers are supposed to project confidence. They're
supposed to have answers, make decisions, know what's
going on with their teams.
This expectation makes it very hard to admit when they
don't know something.
"I'm worried about Sarah, but I'm not sure why." That's not
something managers say out loud. It sounds uncertain. It
invites questions they can't answer. It suggests they're not
fully in control of their team.
So they keep the uncertainty to themselves. They watch
Sarah and wonder if something's wrong. They tell
themselves it's probably nothing. They wait for clearer
evidence before raising a concern that might make them
look like they don't have a handle on things.
The clearer evidence arrives in the form of a resignation
letter.
This is the confidence problem. The culture of
management rewards certainty and punishes doubt.
Managers learn to project confidence even when they
don't have it. Especially when they don't have it.
The result is that early warning signs stay hidden. The
manager who senses something but can't prove it stays

Section 4

quiet. The executive who might have helped never learns
there was a problem.
Managers aren't supposed to have doubts. So they keep
their doubts to themselves until the doubts become
resignations.
What Managers Can't See From Where
They Sit
A manager sees their team. They see the one-on-ones, the
project updates, the mood in team meetings. They see
their slice of the organization.
They don't see the other slices.
They don't know that the engineer who seems fine has
been talking to three other managers about transferring.
They don't know that the designer who stopped pushing
back did the same thing on their last team before quitting.
Each manager operates in isolation. They have deep
context on their own team and almost no context on
anything else.
When HR sees turnover patterns across departments,
managers don't see that data. When exit interviews reveal
recurring themes, managers don't see those themes.
When someone's behavior matches a pattern that's

Section 4

preceded resignation in other cases, the manager has no
way to know.
They're making decisions with a fraction of the available
information. They're trying to prevent departures without
knowing what departure warning signs look like across the
organization.
It's like asking someone to navigate a city having only seen
their own neighborhood. They can be excellent at
understanding their block. They'll still get lost the moment
they step outside it.
The Skip-Level That Didn't Happen

The engineer thought about using it. She had concerns

seemed like the right move.
She looked at the VP's calendar. Booked solid for weeks.
She drafted an email requesting time. Deleted it. Drafted it
again. Deleted it again.

What if it got back to her manager? What if she raised

The skip-level never happened. She resigned three

door is open." The unwritten rules say "but there will be
consequences if you use it."
Employees know this. They've watched what happens to

difference between what's encouraged and what's actually

The VP never knew there was a problem. From their
perspective, no news was good news. The door was open.
Nobody walked through it. Everything must be fine.
Fighting a Battle Nobody Knows About
The manager spent three weeks fighting for Sarah's
promotion. Wrote the justification. Gathered the data.
Made the case in two separate meetings. Got pushback
from finance about headcount. Made the case again.
Finally got it approved.
Sarah never knew any of this happened.

Section 4

From Sarah's perspective, she asked about her promotion
and then waited. Eventually it came through. She assumed
it was routine. She didn't know her manager had gone to
war for it.
This happens constantly. Managers fight battles their
teams never see. They advocate in rooms their employees
aren't in. They push for raises, transfers, opportunities, and
absorb the friction without passing it on.
When they win, the employee assumes things just worked
out. When they lose, the employee assumes the manager
didn't try.
There's no visibility into the fight. No way for the employee
to know what their manager did on their behalf. No way to
build trust through demonstrated advocacy because the
advocacy happens behind closed doors.
Managers accumulate invisible scar tissue from battles
nobody knows about. They win some and lose some, and
either way, the effort disappears into the system.
Eventually, some of them stop fighting. Not because they
stopped caring. Because the fights were never seen, and
the losses were never understood.
When Caring Becomes Career Risk
The manager who cares too much becomes a problem.

Section 4

They escalate concerns that leadership doesn't want to
hear. They push for budget that doesn't exist. They
advocate loudly for people in ways that make them seem
like they can't manage their team's expectations.
At some point, someone pulls them aside. "You need to be
more strategic about what you raise. Not everything needs
to go up the chain. You need to manage your team's
expectations better."
The translation: stop caring so loudly. It's making things
difficult.
So they learn. They stop raising every concern. They
absorb frustration instead of escalating it. They tell their
team "I'll see what I can do" instead of fighting battles they
know they'll lose.
They become better organizational players. They become
worse advocates.
The ones who don't learn eventually leave. They go
somewhere that values the caring, or they burn out trying
to care in a system that punishes it. Either way, the
organization loses the managers who were willing to fight
for their people.
What remains are the managers who learned the lesson.
The ones who care quietly, or not at all. The ones who
know that fighting too hard is a career risk.

Section 5

What Actually Works

Section 5

Six Things That Make People Stay
People don't leave jobs. They leave situations where they
feel unheard, stuck, invisible, unsupported, or
disconnected.
The research points to six factors that determine whether
someone stays or goes. Not compensation. Not perks. Not
the quality of the snacks in the break room.
The factors are simpler than that.
Do they feel like they can communicate honestly with their
manager? Do they feel like they're learning and growing?
Do they see opportunity ahead of them? Do they feel safe
being vulnerable about challenges? Do they have what
they need to do their job well? Do they have time and
space to reflect on how things are going?
Six questions. The answers predict retention better than
any engagement survey.
When all six are healthy, people stay even when recruiters
call. When one or more breaks down, they start thinking
about leaving. When multiple break down at once, the
resignation is already being drafted.
These aren't complicated concepts. They're basic human
needs applied to work. The problem isn't that companies
don't understand them. The problem is that nobody's
watching whether they're being met.

Section 5

The manager doesn't have visibility. The employee doesn't
raise concerns. The breakdown happens in silence until it
becomes a resignation.
What works is making the invisible visible. Before it's too
late.
Daily, Not Annual
Annual surveys measure how people felt months ago. By
the time you see the data, the moment has passed. The
employee who was frustrated in February filled out the
survey. By July, when you're reviewing results, they've
already accepted another offer.
The cadence is wrong.
Engagement doesn't move on an annual cycle. It moves
daily. Someone has a bad interaction with their manager
on Tuesday, and by Thursday they're wondering if they
should update their resume. Someone gets passed over
for a project on Monday, and by the following Monday
they're talking to a recruiter.
The interventions that work happen in the same timeframe
as the problems. Not months later. Days later. Sometimes
hours later.
This doesn't mean pestering employees with daily surveys.
It means having systems that surface signals in real time.

Section 5

A manager who notices a pattern shift this week, not this
quarter. A conversation that happens while the frustration
is still fresh, not after it's hardened into a decision.
Annual measurement is for board decks. Daily awareness
is for retention.
The companies that actually prevent turnover aren't the
ones with the best annual surveys. They're the ones who
know what's happening right now, on every team, before
small problems become resignations.
Small Actions, Repeated
The interventions that prevent turnover aren't dramatic.
They're small. A five-minute conversation. A question
asked at the right moment. A piece of feedback delivered
before the frustration builds.
None of these things are hard to do. The problem is that
they're easy to skip.
When a manager has twelve direct reports and eight hours
of meetings, the five-minute conversation gets pushed to
next week. The question that should be asked today gets
forgotten by tomorrow. The feedback that would have
helped arrives too late to matter.
Small actions only work if they happen consistently. A
single good conversation doesn't build trust. A hundred

Section 5

good conversations do. A single moment of recognition
doesn't make someone feel valued. A pattern of
recognition does.
This is why programs fail and systems succeed. Programs
create events. Systems create patterns. A manager who
has one great development conversation per quarter isn't
moving the needle. A manager who has small, consistent
touchpoints every week is.
The math is simple. Small actions, repeated over time,
compound into relationships that can withstand frustration.
Small actions, skipped repeatedly, compound into
distance that ends in resignation.
What works isn't doing something big once. It's doing
something small every time.
Communication: The Conversation
That Should Have Happened
The engineer had concerns about the project timeline. She
mentioned it once in a team meeting. The manager
nodded and moved on to the next agenda item.
She didn't bring it up again. Neither did he.
Four months later, she resigned. In her exit interview, she
mentioned feeling unheard. The timeline concern was just

Section 5

the surface. Underneath was a pattern: she'd raise things,
they'd be acknowledged but not addressed, and eventually
she stopped raising them.
This is what communication breakdown looks like. Not
shouting matches or obvious conflict. Quiet erosion.
Things mentioned once and not followed up on. A slow
fade from dialogue to monologue.
The conversation that should have happened was simple.
"You mentioned concerns about the timeline last week. I
want to make sure I understand what you're seeing." Two
sentences. Thirty seconds. The signal that her input
mattered.
That conversation didn't happen. Not because the
manager didn't care. Because the moment passed, and
there was no system to bring it back.
Communication isn't about having an open-door policy. It's
about closing loops. Following up. Making sure that when
someone raises something, they know it was heard and
what happens next.
Most managers think they communicate well. Most
employees disagree.

Learning: The Growth Path That
Disappeared
When he started, the growth path was clear. Learn the
systems, take on bigger projects, eventually move into a
senior role. The trajectory made sense.
Somewhere along the way, it stopped making sense.
The bigger projects went to someone else. The senior role
discussion kept getting pushed to next quarter. The skills
he was building didn't seem to connect to any obvious next
step.
He didn't complain. He just quietly concluded that growth
wasn't going to happen here. Started looking for
somewhere it would.
This is how learning breaks down. Not with a dramatic
refusal to invest in development. With a gradual
disappearance of forward motion. The employee stops
seeing a path, and nobody notices because they're still
doing their current job just fine.
The fix isn't complicated. It's making the growth path visible
and keeping it visible. Not once a year in a development
review. Regularly. “Here’s what you’re building toward.
Here’s what comes next.”
When employees can see their future at the company,
they're less likely to go looking for one somewhere else.

Section 5

When the path disappears into vague promises and
perpetual delays, they start drawing new paths that lead
out the door.
Learning isn't about training budgets. It's about trajectory.
Opportunity: The Question They
Stopped Asking
For the first two years, she asked about opportunity
constantly. What's the path to senior? When might a team
lead role open up? What would she need to demonstrate
to be considered?
Her manager gave vague answers. "We'll see how things
develop." "Let's revisit next quarter." "There might be
something coming up."
By year three, she stopped asking.
Her manager interpreted this as patience. She'd settled in.
Understood that these things take time. Wasn't being
pushy about advancement anymore.
That wasn't what happened. She stopped asking because
she stopped believing the answers would be any different.
The questions had led nowhere, so she stopped wasting
energy on them.

Section 5

The silence wasn't acceptance. It was resignation in the
original sense of the word: giving up.
When employees stop asking about opportunity, most
managers feel relief. One less difficult conversation. One
less expectation to manage. What they don't realize is that
the questions didn't go away. They just moved. From the
manager's office to the recruiter's inbox.
Opportunity doesn't require immediate promotion. It
requires honest conversation about what's possible and
when. Employees can wait for the right role if they believe
it's coming. What they can't do is wait indefinitely for
something that's never clearly defined.
The question they stopped asking is the one that should
worry you most.
Vulnerability: When "I'm Fine" Means
"I'm Done"
"How are things going?" "Fine."
The manager moved on. The employee was fine. No
problems here.
Except "fine" is almost never fine. It's what people say when
they don't feel safe saying anything else. When honesty

Section 5

feels risky. When they've learned that raising problems
creates more problems than it solves.
"Fine" is the wall employees put up when vulnerability feels
too dangerous.
This is the trap. The manager needs to know what's really
happening in order to help. The employee needs to feel
safe in order to share what's really happening. If the
environment doesn't support vulnerability, the manager
never gets the information they need.
The result is a relationship built on pleasant fictions.
Everything seems fine until suddenly it isn't. The
resignation arrives and the manager is blindsided because
they thought things were going well.
Creating space for vulnerability isn't about being soft. It's
about being accurate. You can't fix problems you don't
know about. You can't retain someone whose concerns
are hidden behind "fine" until the day they resign.
The organizations that retain talent are the ones where
people can say "I'm struggling with this" without fear of
being judged, labeled, or penalized.
Everything else is guesswork.

Enablement: The Tools They Don't Have
She knew what needed to be done. She just couldn't do it.
The system she needed access to required approval from
three different departments. The budget for the contractor
who could help was frozen until next quarter. Every day
was a series of workarounds. Finding ways to do the job
despite the obstacles rather than because of the support.
She mentioned it a few times. Nothing changed. Eventually
she stopped mentioning it and started interviewing.
This is enablement failure. Not a lack of skill or motivation.
A lack of the basic resources, access, and support needed
to do the job well.
Most managers assume that if someone has the title, they
have what they need. They don't ask whether the tools are
actually there. Whether the access actually works.
Whether the support actually materializes.
The employee knows. They experience the friction every
day. They know exactly what's missing and exactly how
much harder it makes everything.
When enablement breaks down, employees face a choice:
keep fighting an uphill battle indefinitely, or go somewhere
the hill isn't as steep.
The fix is simple in concept. Ask people what they need to
do their job well. Then actually provide it.
